claims.text: Elemental Cr coatings directly on zirconium-alloy substrates are prone to Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
Directly coated Cr/Zr-alloy systems experience significant Cr–Zr interdiffusion under accident-relevant high-temperature conditions.
Cr–Zr interdiffusion accelerates degradation of the coating system under accident-relevant high-temperature conditions.
A 50–100 nm TiN layer at the Cr/Zr-alloy interface will act as a diffusion barrier.
The TiN layer can remain continuous and adherent at the Cr/Zr-alloy interface under the stated environments.
A continuous TiN layer provides a physical boundary that limits atomic diffusion between Cr and Zr.
TiN has sufficiently high thermal stability for the proposed elevated-temperature application.
Cr and Zr have sufficiently low diffusivity through TiN for a 50–100 nm TiN layer to reduce their mutual diffusion at elevated temperature.
Reducing Cr–Zr mutual diffusion will inhibit the formation and growth of deleterious interdiffusion zones or intermetallic phases.
Cr–Zr interdiffusion zones or intermetallic phases can compromise coating integrity.
The TiN interlayer will prevent premature coating failure during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure.
After steam exposure at temperatures of at least 900°C for up to one hour, the TiN-interfaced system will have a notably thinner Cr–Zr interdiffusion zone than the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
The TiN-interfaced system will retain subcritical-water corrosion performance comparable to that of the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
Approximately 290°C water exposure for thousands of hours represents the relevant normal-operation boundary for this hypothesis.
Steam exposure at temperatures of at least 900°C for approximately 30–60 minutes represents the relevant accident boundary for this hypothesis.
Barrier-thickness variations or minor processing deviations may affect long-term stability and performance under cyclic thermal loading.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the TiN layer will prevent Cr–Zr interdiffusion, whereas the mechanism and predicted outcome only claim reduced diffusion and a thinner interdiffusion zone. The falsification rule likewise requires only a 'marked reduction,' so the intended endpoint alternates between prevention and mitigation.
